groups.text: The card issuer is having a bad day.
Each charge waits two seconds for a timeout, then fails.
Your callers wait for nothing, and the issuer gets no room to recover.
A circuit breaker stops calling it for a while.
It wraps every call to the issuer, the way a decorator does.
And it is always in one of three states.
Closed is the normal state.
Calls pass through, and the breaker counts failures in a row.
A success sets the count back to zero.
Now the issuer goes down again, and fails three times in a row.
The third failure trips the breaker.
It opens, until thirty seconds from now.
Open means calls fail fast.
The breaker throws CallNotPermitted at once, with no network trip.
Your callers get a quick answer, and the issuer gets room to recover.
When the cool-down ends, the breaker goes half-open.
It lets one trial call through, and that call decides.
If it succeeds, the breaker closes.
If it fails, the breaker opens again, for another thirty seconds.
Every request thread shares this one breaker.
So the state lives in one AtomicReference.
Each state is a small immutable record, and the reference only changes by compare-and-set.
Compare-and-set takes the record you read, and a new one.
It swaps the new one in only if the reference still holds the one you read.
The breaker opened with a thirty-second cool-down.
In a test, an injected clock jumps thirty-one seconds ahead, and eight threads call at the same moment.
Each one reads Open, sees that the cool-down is over, and calls compareAndSet, from that Open to HalfOpen.
Exactly one wins, and runs the probe.
For the other seven, the reference no longer holds the Open they read.
Their compareAndSet fails, and they get CallNotPermitted.
With a plain set, all eight would get through, to an issuer that may still be down.
In code, it is a few lines, the same in Java and in Kotlin.
Read the state.
If it is Open and the time is up, try compareAndSet to HalfOpen, and throw if you lose.
So the breaker is three patterns in one class: sealed states, a wrapper around every call, and one AtomicReference that changes only by compare-and-set.
